h1: The 6 Best 5GHz Wi-Fi Extenders of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 6 dual-band 5GHz Wi-Fi extenders scored on 5GHz speed, Wi-Fi standard, ports and honest coverage claims.
summary: The TP-Link AX3000 is the strongest 5GHz extender here, with Wi-Fi 6, a 2404 Mbps headline rate and directional antennas. The TP-Link AX1800 RE615X is the sensible Wi-Fi 6 step with an Ethernet port. The AC1900 RE550 is the best Wi-Fi 5 value, and the AC1200 RE315 is the cheapest dependable entry. The two budget repeaters with 5000 square foot claims need a skeptical read.
intro: The number on the box is the least useful figure on a Wi-Fi extender. An AC1200 label adds a 300 Mbps 2.4GHz band to an 867 Mbps 5GHz band, and no device can use both at once. What you can actually count on is the 5GHz rate, and the fact that a single-radio extender spends half of that talking to your router and half talking to your phone.

We reviewed six dual-band extenders from the spec sheets, ranking them on 5GHz rate, Wi-Fi generation, wired ports and how plausible each coverage claim is. The ordering leans toward Wi-Fi 6 and Ethernet, since an extender with a wired port can feed a console or TV without using the wireless link at all.

products.name: TP-Link AX3000 WiFi 6 Range Extender
products.verdict: The only extender here with a 2404 Mbps headline rate and Wi-Fi 6.
products.description:
The AX3000 is a Wi-Fi 6 dual-band extender with a 3 Gbps total rating and a 2404 Mbps headline rate on the faster band. TP-Link lists coverage of up to 2400 square feet and uses two high-gain directional antennas with beamforming, which aims signal at devices rather than spraying it evenly.

It tops the ranking on rate alone. The next TP-Link, the AX1800, cuts the headline figure to 1.8 Gbps, and both AC models drop to Wi-Fi 5. Directional antennas are the other differentiator: placing the unit correctly matters more here than on an omni-antenna model, because the beam has a front and a back.

Buy it if your router is Wi-Fi 6 and you have fast internet to protect. The $100 to $200 bucket is the steepest in the group, so skip it if your devices are all older Wi-Fi 5 clients.
pros: Highest headline rate in the group
products.idealFor: Wi-Fi 6 households with a fast internet plan.
products.skipIf: Your router and phones are older Wi-Fi 5 gear.

products.name: TP-Link AX1800 RE615X
products.verdict: Wi-Fi 6 plus an Ethernet port, at half the AX3000's bucket.
products.description:
The RE615X is a Wi-Fi 6 dual-band extender rated at 1.8 Gbps total with up to 2100 square feet of listed coverage and an Ethernet port. It sits in the $50 to $100 bucket.

The Ethernet port is the feature that moves it ahead of the Wi-Fi 5 AC1900. A wired port lets you plug a TV, console or desktop into the extender, which leaves the wireless link free for everything else. Compared with the AX3000, you lose roughly 1.2 Gbps of headline rate and about 300 square feet of listed range, but you also save a bucket.

Buy it for a mid-size home with a Wi-Fi 6 router and a stationary device to wire up. The honest caveat is that the 5GHz rate is not listed separately, so check your router band before assuming full speed.
products.idealFor: Mid-size homes with Wi-Fi 6 routers and a TV to wire.
products.skipIf: You want maximum throughput for gigabit internet.

products.name: TP-Link AC1900 RE550
products.verdict: Three adjustable antennas and 1.9 Gbps on Wi-Fi 5 for under $50.
products.description:
The RE550 is a Wi-Fi 5 dual-band extender with a 1.9 Gbps total rating, 2100 square feet of listed coverage and three adjustable external antennas. It sits in the $25 to $50 bucket.

Its total bandwidth is the second highest in the group, but the standard is older, so the AX1800 delivers better behavior with multiple modern devices at a higher bucket. The external antennas can be angled, which helps when the outlet position is poor. It beats the AC1200 RE315 on rate and coverage for a small step up in price.

Buy it if your router and devices are Wi-Fi 5 and you want an affordable boost. The 1.9 Gbps figure combines both bands, so do not expect it on a single phone.
products.idealFor: Wi-Fi 5 households that want more reach cheaply.
products.skipIf: You need a wired port or Wi-Fi 6 features.

products.name: TP-Link AC1200 RE315
products.verdict: 867 Mbps on 5GHz for under $25, from a brand with firmware support.
products.description:
The RE315 is an AC1200 extender: 867 Mbps on 5GHz plus 300 Mbps on 2.4GHz, with 1500 square feet of listed coverage and two adjustable external antennas. TP-Link lists Adaptive Path Selection, a feature intended to pick the best route between router and extender. It is in the under $25 bucket.

The 5GHz figure of 867 Mbps is the number to weigh, and it is the same as the PEDUMMY's. Where it separates from the two generic repeaters is brand: TP-Link firmware and app support are better documented than the unnamed alternatives. It ranks below the RE550 on bandwidth and coverage.

Buy it for a small apartment or a single dead room. The 1500 square foot claim is the smallest in the group, so do not stretch it across a large house.
products.idealFor: Small apartments and single weak rooms.
products.skipIf: Your home is large or you need wired ports.

products.name: PEDUMMY 1200Mbps WiFi Extender
products.verdict: 867 Mbps on 5GHz, an Ethernet port and AP mode, with an optimistic range claim.
products.description:
The PEDUMMY lists 867 Mbps on 5GHz and 300 Mbps on 2.4GHz, an Ethernet port, an access point mode and up to 5200 square feet of coverage. It is in the $25 to $50 bucket.

The wired port and AP mode are real advantages: you can run a cable from the router and create a proper second access point, which avoids the halving penalty of wireless repeating. But 5200 square feet is not a figure the antenna count supports, and no brand support page backs it up. It ranks above the VERMEYEN because the Ethernet port and AP mode are explicit, but below the TP-Link models for firmware track record.

Buy it if you can run Ethernet to it. Treat the coverage claim as a marketing number and plan for a fraction of it.
pros: Access point mode for wired setups
products.idealFor: Wired access-point setups on a low budget.
products.skipIf: You want a branded product with documented updates.

products.name: VERMEYEN 1200Mbps 5G WiFi Extender
products.verdict: Three selectable modes, but the lightest spec detail in the group.
products.description:
The VERMEYEN is a 1200 Mbps dual-band extender with 300 Mbps on 2.4GHz, a 5000 square foot listed coverage claim and three selectable modes, including repeater and AP. It sits in the $25 to $50 bucket.

Mode flexibility is the attraction, and it is why the unit is on the list at all. It ranks last because the listing does not break out the 5GHz rate, mention a wired port or provide a brand track record, which leaves less to verify than the PEDUMMY. Like that model, the 5000 square foot figure is a ceiling, not a typical result.

Buy it if you like switching between repeater and access-point use. Skip it if you want hard numbers to compare, as the 5GHz rate and any Ethernet connection are not clearly listed.
products.idealFor: Tinkerers who want to switch between modes.
products.skipIf: You need documented speeds or a wired port.

methodology.title: 5GHz throughput
methodology.description: The rated 5GHz speed or the nearest stated figure, since this band carries most of the real traffic and backhaul.

methodology.title: Wi-Fi standard
methodology.description: Wi-Fi 6 versus Wi-Fi 5, because the newer standard handles many devices more efficiently.

methodology.title: Wired options
methodology.description: Ethernet ports and access point mode, which move traffic off the wireless link and avoid repeater slowdown.

methodology.title: Coverage realism
methodology.description: How plausible the listed square footage is for the antenna design and brand, discounting inflated claims.

methodology.title: Brand and support
methodology.description: Documented firmware, app support and warranty, which decide how long the extender stays useful.

whatMatters.detail: Total bandwidth adds both bands together, but your phone connects to one band at a time. The 5GHz figure, such as 867 Mbps on the RE315, is the one that matters for streaming and calls. Look for it as a separate line in the listing, not just the AC or AX total in the title.

Wi-Fi 6 improves efficiency when many devices share the connection, even if peak speed looks similar on paper. The AX3000 and AX1800 offer it, the RE550 and RE315 do not. Check your router's standard first, because a Wi-Fi 5 router limits what a Wi-Fi 6 extender can deliver, and look for the standard on the box.

A single-radio extender uses the same airtime to talk to the router and to your devices, which roughly halves throughput. A wired Ethernet port or AP mode avoids that. The RE615X, PEDUMMY and VERMEYEN offer wired or AP options; confirm the port on the listing photos.

Square footage claims are lab-style ceilings under ideal conditions, with no walls or interference. The TP-Link figures of 1500 to 2400 sq ft are believable for a small unit, while 5000 and 5200 are not. Place any extender halfway between the router and the dead zone, where it still receives a strong signal, and discount the claim by half.

Adjustable external antennas, as on the RE550 and RE315, let you angle signal toward the weak area. Directional antennas, as on the AX3000, concentrate it in one direction. Match the design to your layout: directional for long hallways, adjustable for awkward outlet positions. Check the listing photos to see whether antennas are fixed or movable.

howToChoose.intro: The standard decides how well the extender behaves with many devices, not only how fast it is.

cards.label: Repeater
cards.text: Rebroadcasts your router wirelessly. Simple, but it shares airtime and cuts throughput. The AC models and the AX1800 work this way by default.

cards.label: Access point
cards.text: Connects by Ethernet and creates a clean second network. The PEDUMMY and VERMEYEN list AP mode, and the AX1800 has an Ethernet port.

howToChoose.note: Use a cable and AP mode whenever you can; fall back to wireless repeating only when running a cable is not an option.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Wi-Fi 6, a high 5GHz rate and an Ethernet port so the console or TV can be wired to the extender.

cards.label: In this ranking
cards.text: The AX1800 RE615X adds the port at a mid-range bucket, and the AX3000 delivers the highest rate if you have fast internet.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Your router is Wi-Fi 6 and your plan is fast. The AX3000's 2404 Mbps headline rate only matters when the rest of the chain can feed it.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You have a small home and Wi-Fi 5 gear. The RE315 and RE550 cover that for under $50.

faq.q: Will a 5GHz extender work with any router?
faq.a: Yes, all six pair with standard routers. The AX3000 and AX1800 are Wi-Fi 6 but fall back to older standards on an older router, so you only get their top speed when the router supports Wi-Fi 6 as well.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake when placing an extender?
faq.a: Putting it in the dead zone itself. The RE550 or AX1800 needs a strong signal from the router first, so plug it halfway between the router and the weak area, where it still sees good signal.

faq.q: Is the AX3000 worth it over the AX1800 RE615X?
faq.a: Only with fast internet and a Wi-Fi 6 router. The AX3000 raises the headline rate to 2404 Mbps and coverage to 2400 sq ft, but the AX1800 gives Wi-Fi 6 and Ethernet at half the cost.

faq.q: How do I set up an extender in AP mode?
faq.a: Connect the PEDUMMY or VERMEYEN to your router by Ethernet, switch to AP mode in its settings and name the network. Do this before relocating it, so you can confirm the wired link works.

faq.q: How do I keep an extender running well over time?
faq.a: Keep firmware current, since TP-Link models like the RE315 receive updates and generic units may not. Restart it every few months, and check its placement if speeds drop after furniture or router changes.

faq.q: Can I use two extenders in one home?
faq.a: Daisy-chaining wireless extenders cuts speed at every hop. If you need more coverage, use one extender with an Ethernet connection, like the RE615X, or step up to a mesh system rather than stacking repeaters.

finalTake: The TP-Link AX3000 is the extender to buy if your router and internet plan are modern. Most homes will be better served by the AX1800 RE615X, which adds Wi-Fi 6 and an Ethernet port for half the bucket. Choose the AC1900 RE550 or AC1200 RE315 for Wi-Fi 5 setups, and treat the 5000 square foot claims on the generic units with caution.
